title: Keyword search: the inverted index and BM25
summary: Embeddings blur rare exact strings such as error codes and product names, which keyword search matches directly. An inverted index maps each word to the documents that contain it, so a query touches only its own words' postings. BM25 scores a document as a sum over query words of an IDF rarity weight times a saturating, length-normalised term count, with k1 setting saturation and b setting length normalisation.
llm_link: Most production RAG systems run BM25 next to dense retrieval, because user questions often hinge on exact identifiers (error codes, SKUs, function names) that an embedding model has rarely seen. The next lesson fuses the two.
key_ideas: An inverted index stores, for every word, a postings list: the documents containing it and how often. A query only reads the postings of its own words.
Term frequency saturates: f·(k1+1)/(f + k1·norm) rises quickly and flattens, so the tenth mention adds far less than the first. k1 (often 1.2-2.0) sets how soon.
IDF weights rare words up: idf = ln(1 + (N − n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5)) for a word in n of N documents (the form Lucene uses). A word in every document weighs almost nothing.
Length normalisation: norm = 1 − b + b·|D|/avgdl. b = 0 ignores length, b = 1 normalises fully; 0.75 is a common default.
BM25 matches surface forms only: 'money back' will not find 'refund'. That is exactly where embeddings help, hence hybrid search.

quiz.q: A user asks about error code E1047. Why might dense (embedding) retrieval miss the right page?
options: Embeddings cannot represent numbers at all
A rare code carries little meaning for the embedding model, so it barely moves the vector, even though it is the exact string that must match
The code is too long to embed
Cosine similarity ignores the first word
quiz.explain: An embedding compresses a passage into a direction of meaning. A code the model has rarely seen contributes little to that direction, while keyword search treats it as a highly informative exact token.

quiz.q: Predict the result: with k1 = 1.2 and length normalisation switched off (norm = 1), how does a word appearing 10 times in a document compare with one appearing once?
quiz.explain: f·(k1+1)/(f+k1): for f = 1 that is 2.2/2.2 = 1.0, and for f = 10 it is 22/11.2 ≈ 1.96, so about twice as much, nowhere near ten times. Saturation caps a word's contribution at k1 + 1 = 2.2 however often it repeats.

quiz.q: A word appears in every one of N documents. Using idf = ln(1 + (N − n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5)), what is its weight, roughly?
quiz.explain: With n = N the fraction is 0.5/(N + 0.5), tiny for large N, so the idf is ln(1 + tiny) ≈ 0. Finding a word that is everywhere is no evidence. (The +1 inside the log keeps it from going negative, which the original formula could.)
norm = 1 − b + b·|D|/avgdl. With b = 0 it is always 1, so a long document's counts are not scaled down. With b = 1 they are scaled fully by |D|/avgdl.

quiz.q: Your RAG assistant answers 'how do I get my money back?' poorly, though a page titled 'Refund policy' exists. Which retriever is most likely missing it, and why?
options: Dense retrieval, because 'refund' is a rare word
BM25, because it matches surface words and 'money back' shares none with 'refund'
Both, because the question is too short
Neither; this is a generation problem
quiz.explain: BM25 needs the same tokens. Paraphrases are exactly what embeddings capture, which is why production systems combine the two retrievers.

problems.title: Build an inverted index
problems.prompt:
Write build_index(docs). docs maps a document id to its text. Return a dict that maps each word to its postings: a dict from document id to how many times the word occurs there.

Use the tokenize function provided, so that "Refund!" and "refund" count as the same word.

build_index({"a": "the cat", "b": "the the dog"})
# {'the': {'a': 1, 'b': 2}, 'cat': {'a': 1}, 'dog': {'b': 1}}

tests.name: counts repeated words
tests.code:
ix = build_index({'a': 'the cat', 'b': 'the the dog'})
assert ix.get('the') == {'a': 1, 'b': 2}, f"'the' should map to {{'a': 1, 'b': 2}}, got {ix.get('the')}"

tests.name: words only in one document
tests.code:
ix = build_index({'a': 'the cat', 'b': 'the the dog'})
assert ix.get('cat') == {'a': 1} and ix.get('dog') == {'b': 1}, f'cat/dog postings are wrong: {ix}'

tests.name: case and punctuation are normalised
tests.code:
ix = build_index({'x': 'Refund! refund, REFUND.'})
assert ix == {'refund': {'x': 3}}, f'expected {{"refund": {{"x": 3}}}} (use tokenize), got {ix}'

tests.name: a word absent from a document is not listed for it
tests.code:
ix = build_index({'a': 'alpha', 'b': 'beta'})
assert 'b' not in ix['alpha'], 'postings must only list documents that contain the word'

hints: Loop: for doc_id, text in docs.items(): for word in tokenize(text): ...
postings = index.setdefault(word, {}) gives you the inner dict, creating it if needed.

problems.title: Score documents with BM25
problems.prompt:
Write bm25_scores(query, index, doc_lens, k1=1.2, b=0.75). It returns a dict from document id to score, for every document that contains at least one query word.

For each query word with postings in n of the N documents, and each document containing it f times:

idf  = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5))
norm = k1 * (1 - b + b * doc_len / avgdl)
score += idf * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + norm)

doc_lens maps each document id to its number of tokens; N is its length and avgdl the mean length. Words missing from the index contribute nothing.

tests.name: matches a hand calculation
tests.code:
import math
ix={'refund':{'a':1}}; lens={'a':10,'b':10}
s=bm25_scores('refund', ix, lens)
idf=math.log(1+(2-1+0.5)/(1+0.5))
exp=idf*1*2.2/(1+1.2)
assert 'a' in s and abs(s['a']-exp)<1e-9, f'expected score {exp:.4f} for doc a, got {s}'

tests.name: rare words outweigh common ones
term frequency saturates
tests.code:
lens={'a':10,'b':10}
s1=bm25_scores('x', {'x':{'a':1}}, lens, b=0)['a']
s10=bm25_scores('x', {'x':{'a':10}}, lens, b=0)['a']
assert s10 < 3*s1, f'10 mentions should score far less than 10x one mention (got ratio {s10/s1:.2f}); did you forget the saturation term?'

tests.name: longer documents are penalised
b = 0 ignores length
unknown words are skipped
tests.code:
s=bm25_scores('zzz', {'x':{'a':1}}, {'a':3})
assert s=={}, f'no document contains zzz, expected {{}}, got {s}'

hints: n = len(postings) is the number of documents that contain the word.
for doc, f in postings.items(): norm = k1 * (1 - b + b * doc_lens[doc] / avgdl)

problems.title: Search a small help centre
problems.prompt:
Put the two pieces together. Write search(query, docs, k=2) that builds an index of docs, scores them with BM25, and returns the ids of the top k documents, best first. Break ties by document id so the order is deterministic.

build_index and bm25_scores are provided in working form. Try the query "refund E1047" on DOCS: which document should win?

tests.name: the exact error code wins
tests.code:
r=search('refund E1047', DOCS)
assert r and r[0]=='d2', f'd2 is the only page with E1047 and should rank first, got {r}'

tests.name: returns k results
tests.code:
r=search('refund', DOCS, k=3)
assert len(r)==3, f'expected 3 ids, got {r}'

tests.name: only matching documents are returned
tests.code:
r=search('shipping', DOCS, k=5)
assert r==['d3'], f'only d3 mentions shipping, got {r}'

tests.name: paraphrase is invisible to BM25
tests.code:
r=search('money back', DOCS)
assert r==[], f'no page contains money or back, so BM25 finds nothing (that is the point), got {r}'
